claims.text: Separately modeling lattice and electronic heat transport will yield total thermal-conductivity estimates within ±10% of experiment over 200–1200 K.
The new approach will outperform earlier methods that conflate lattice and electronic heat transport.
The target material is homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The target material has minimal defects.
The proposed approach separately treats phonon-mediated and electron-mediated heat transport.
The proposed approach combines atomic-scale simulations with semi-empirical corrections.
Relevant structural mediators include local chemical variations produced by atomic-scale disorder.
Oxygen impurities induce defects that scatter heat carriers.
Independent treatment of lattice and electronic contributions captures temperature-dependent scattering.
Independent treatment of the two transport channels captures defect interactions missed by conflated models.
Capturing temperature-dependent scattering and defect interactions improves the fidelity of thermal-conductivity predictions.
The approach will reduce predictive error by at least 20% relative to methods that do not decouple lattice and electronic transport.
Below 200 K, the model should predict near parity between lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Existing analytical and simulation methods use idealized defect-free models or conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Existing methods typically incur predictive errors of 20–50%.
The hypothesis applies only to HfNbTaTiZr with controlled impurity levels and a uniform microstructure.
The predictions are valid only between 200 and 1200 K.
Predictive performance may vary with sample preparation and minor compositional variations.

contradictions.description: The prediction includes near parity below 200 K, but the stated validity boundary excludes all temperatures below 200 K.
Measurements are specified only from 200 to 1200 K, yet the design calls for a decisive low-temperature comparison below 200 K.

The headline ±10% claim concerns total thermal conductivity, whereas the falsification rule also requires each separately estimated lattice and electronic contribution to fall within ±10%, imposing a stronger criterion not stated in the main hypothesis.
